# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

whys.g1: Leaving all three on their own is right, because trying a pair at a matinee, catching audience questions in a big hall, and taking the end seat for one-sided hearing are three different things that I wouldn't put together, and no group exists that any of them should have joined.
whys.g2: No answer was grouped, so nothing was presented as being about this, but Tomás's end-seat answer doesn't say what would make it worth it and is borderline off-topic, though it was at least left on its own.

founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the identical question, 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Nothing asks about the commercial side: the price ($599 for the glasses, plus the $20/month Pro plan), who decides and pays, what people spend today on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, or HSA/FSA eligibility. The only commercial touch is the pilot offer on screen 19. Nothing asks what access my respondents need either, and because they are deaf and hard of hearing, the answer format on screen 21 must work without hearing, so I would need to be asked about captions, text or ASL.

screens.why2: The hint makes it clear, but "pilot" is a word for a hardware founder selling $599 glasses that suggests a run of units I'd have to supply, while the line itself only asks for an email, so I need a second read to see what I'm agreeing to.
screens.why3: It's my own decision about my own launch, and I can answer it at once because collecting emails from people who would try the glasses is what I want.
screens.why4: Yes and no are the only two answers, they are distinct and plain, and no escape chip is needed for a founder's own choice.
screens.why5: My "Yes" is kept, but the generic "try this for real" says nothing of my commitment step, ordering a pair with free returns, so it could mean a free trial I don't offer.
screens.instead: Ask people at the end if they'd like to try this for real? They'd see: "Would you try this for real? Leave your email." You see who said yes on the Pilot tab. Options: Yes, ask them / No, don't ask

screens.why1: Choosing the interviewer just before launch makes sense in the flow, but for a study of deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, choosing a voice is an odd question to get without first being asked how they can take the interview.
screens.why2: Picking a face is clear at once, but I need a second read for 'Keel records her once for this project' and the two uses of 'her', which point to different people.
screens.why3: I can pick the face I prefer, but I can only guess how well either voice would work for people with hearing loss, and a voice is not what decides that for my respondents.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct, but my true answer is missing because there is no captioned or text-only interview, which many of my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents would need.
screens.why5: My preselected Daphne is kept, but a spoken interviewer drifts from the segment I typed, deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, because it ignores that they may not be able to follow her.
screens.instead: Your respondents are deaf or hard of hearing, so how should they take the interview: Read and type (no voice) / Daphne speaking, with live captions / Saskia speaking, with live captions?

screens.why1: Choosing how people answer belongs just before sending, but it comes right after "Who should ask them your questions?", and Daphne asking aloud partly reopens that choice.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but "Every answer in a quiet room. More than 9 in 10 where it is loud" never says it means answers being captured, and the stray "recording" label takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know my respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, so I can immediately pick text over a video that asks its questions aloud.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and my true answer, Text only, is there, but Daphne is described with no mention of captions for my deaf respondents, and the "recording" label on Let them choose is unexplained.
screens.why5: My pick of Text only is shown as typed, and nothing on the screen changes what I said about my product or the people in the study.
screens.instead: How should they answer? Text only: they read each question and tap or type. AI interviewer (Daphne): she asks each question on video, with captions on screen, and they can talk, type or tap. Let them choose: they pick Daphne or text when they open the link.

screens.why1: Having just chosen how people answer, the last thing I need to settle before sending is who receives the link, so it is obvious why it comes here.
screens.why2: "Who gets a link?" and the three options are plain to me on first reading, though "the Contacts page" is a Keel term I can place from the wording around it.
screens.why3: I know whether I am sending to deaf and hard-of-hearing people I can name, finding them through a search, or posting in a community where they already gather.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the ways I would reach people, including a group link for deaf and hard-of-hearing communities, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my pick of people I know by name, and nothing here changes what I typed about the wearer, the job or the glasses.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title, "3 of 3 holding" backs it, and each card puts its own count beside its status, so I know the answer and what decides it.
screens.why_b2: The stage page draws no chart, but the count lines show what is counted and over 7 people; the bar is missing, so I can't tell whether 4 of 7 on adoption cleared it comfortably or barely.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, word for word, even though the statement above them is garbled and repeats itself.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this result means for the idea or what to do next, and the pairing condition on the adoption card is left for me to act on by inference.
screens.why_b5: The 7 stays visible, but nobody says 7 is a small sample, and a flat "Holding up" on adoption at 4 of 7, with 3 more conditional, reads firmer than the data allows.
screens.instead: Holding up, from only 7 people: everyone would have followed more with the glasses, but adoption is the weak spot at 4 of 7 (bar shown), with 3 more only if pairing takes a minute and stays connected, so make pairing fast and reliable and test it with more people before relying on this.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "7 of 7 said yes, easily or with some steps", so the verdict and the number that decides it are side by side and agree.
screens.why_b2: The four answer bars and 7 people are plain, but the bar line only repeats my belief, so I need a second look to infer that "most" is the bar and that "with some steps" counts as a yes.
screens.why_b3: The Compatibility name and the belief line are exactly what I checked on the way in, phone with them and online.
screens.why_b4: The screen stops at the verdict and the names, never saying what this means for the glasses or that 3 of 7 needing some steps is worth a look before I move on.
screens.why_b5: The 7 is visible and every answer is listed, but "For most deaf and hard-of-hearing adults" with "Holding up" reads wider than seven people, and it never says 7 is a small group or that 3 of them needed steps inside the headline yes.
screens.instead: Holding up among the 7 who answered, a small group: all had their phone with them and online, 4 easily and 3 with some steps, so the phone-and-internet requirement isn't blocking anyone here; find out what those steps were before relying on captions starting quickly.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "7 of 7 said it would have gone better, 7 of them a lot", so the verdict and its deciding number are side by side and agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart's title and "Better · 7" show what is counted and over how many, but the bar is missing: the "You said" line only repeats my benefit, and the one-in-three limit I saw on the way in is not drawn or stated.
screens.why_b3: The name Relative advantage and the belief line are exactly the ones I checked, including "following more without asking anyone to repeat".
screens.why_b4: The card never says what this result means for AirCaps or what I should do next; it stops at the count and the list of names.
screens.why_b5: The count of 7 stays visible and nothing claims beyond those people, but the small n is never called small, and a unanimous hypothetical "a lot better" asked with the idea in mind is shown with no caution beside a "For most" belief.
screens.instead: Holding up: 7 of 7 said AirCaps would have made their last conversation better, against a limit of no more than 1 in 3 saying "no difference" or "worse"; that is only 7 people imagining it, so keep following more without asking anyone to repeat as the lead promise and test it on real conversations with the glasses on.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "4 of 7 would do it", and since my belief said most, 4 of 7 plainly decides it.
screens.why_b2: The counts and the seven people are plain from the bars and the "4 of 7" line, but the bar line only repeats my belief, so I have to work out for myself that the bar is a majority and that the 3 conditional answers don't count toward it.
screens.why_b3: The name Adoption friction and the line "Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone" are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for AirCaps or what to do next, and the only implied task, making pairing quick and stable, isn't what these three people asked for.
screens.why_b5: The headline and chart say 3 people would adopt only if pairing took a minute and stayed connected, but their rows read "if it was clearly worth it" and their quotes concern stage lights, audience questions and one-sided deafness, so the data can't carry that condition, and the low n of 7 isn't flagged either.
screens.instead: Holding up, narrowly: 4 of 7 of the people who answered would wear the glasses paired to their phone, which clears the majority bar; the other 3 would if it was clearly worth it, and none mentioned pairing, so show them it works where they need it, starting with a one-matinee trial and audience questions in big halls, before you spend time on pairing.

screens.why_b1: The status "Holding up" and "Adoption friction held, 7 of 7" sit together at the top, so I get the verdict and its deciding number at once.
screens.why_b3: The dimension name is the one I checked, but my line "Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone" is missing, and the "clearly worth it" question is about value more than wearing and pairing.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for the idea, so I have to work out the trial-before-order and audience-pickup implications from the quotes myself.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and no claim reaches beyond those who answered, but a flat "held, 7 of 7" hides that the adoption card had only 4 unconditional and 3 only if pairing was quick and stable.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I did not type: a theatregoer wants to borrow a pair for one matinee to test lens legibility under stage lights, a seminar-goer wants audience questions picked up in big halls, and a one-side-deaf user already copes by taking the end seat.
screens.instead: Adoption friction held at 7 of 7, but only 4 would do it as is and 3 need pairing that takes a minute and stays connected; among the comments, one wants to trial a pair at a matinee before ordering, one wants audience questions picked up in big halls, and one already copes without it, so test a try-before-you-buy offer and hall pickup with more people.

screens.why1: It is the first screen, and asking whether I talk with hearing people is an obvious way to check that this study is for someone like me.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I and other deaf people say it, so I understand the question on first reading, though "talk" doesn't say whether it means face to face.
screens.why3: This is my ordinary week, and I know without guessing that I deal with hearing people at shops, at work and with family.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for a weekly-habit question, and the gate correctly has no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment wording and shows me nothing of a product or plan, and "hearing people" is my own term.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and two options, so I could catch it the first time, though "I'll read 2 options" is a little stiff for a yes-or-no.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: After asking if I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask if I lost track of a conversation with them this past week.
screens.why2: "Lose track of a conversation" is how I would say it myself, and I get it on first reading.
screens.why3: This happens to me all the time, so I can easily answer for the last 7 days.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but there are two escape chips on a screen that needs none, and "I can't recall one particular conversation" is wordy and doesn't suit a question about the whole week.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product leaks to me, but the question drops "face to face" and "too fast or too noisy", so losing track on a video call or for another reason would also count.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it is one short question ending in "Yes or no", and I could answer after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, was a face-to-face conversation with hearing people too fast or too noisy for you to follow? Yes or no, with no chips.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I lost track of a conversation, and under a heading that says an idea is coming, it is obvious why I am being shown this now.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and a lens are everyday words to me, and the only odd bit is 'AirCaps', which the card explains straight away.
screens.why3: It describes the fast, noisy conversations I actually have, and looking away to read captions is something I know well, so I can picture it from my own life.
screens.why4: This is a card to read, with no options to choose from.
screens.why5: It is a deliberate idea card, so naming the product is fine, and the belief is clearly marked as the builders' own rather than slipped in as fact.
screens.why6: It says well in short sentences, but 'Imagine AirCaps' is a strange opener to hear cold, the name could be misheard as 'air caps', and 'the wearer' sounds stiff after being addressed as 'you'.
screens.instead: Imagine glasses called AirCaps. When a conversation with hearing people is too fast or too noisy, you wear them, and live captions of what people nearby are saying show inside the lens. The people building it believe you could read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: After the idea, I can see they want to know if my phone would be there for it, but it comes abruptly because nothing says why the phone matters.
screens.why2: The words are easy, but "your last conversation" doesn't say with hearing people, and "with you and online" asks two things, since I can have my phone with me and no signal.
screens.why3: I know whether I had my phone on me and working the last time I talked with someone.
screens.why4: "Only with help or approval" is nonsense for my own phone because nobody approves me using it, and "Yes, with some steps" doesn't clearly mean anything for simply having a phone on me.
screens.why5: No product plan or role words reach me beyond the idea card, but the conversation has drifted from one with hearing people to any conversation, and the options sound like they were written for a workplace.
screens.why6: It is short and one breath, and I could hold the four options and the escape if I heard it or followed it on the captions.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Did you have your phone with you, working and online? Yes, ready to use; Yes, but no signal or battery; No, I didn't have it. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After being shown the idea and asked about my last conversation, it makes obvious sense to ask whether this would have helped in that conversation.
screens.why2: The question is short and clear, but on this screen 'AirCaps' is only a name, so I have to remember from the earlier card what it does.
screens.why3: I know how my last conversation went, but I have not used AirCaps, so I would be partly guessing how much it would have helped.
screens.why4: The options run cleanly from a lot better to worse, use words I would use, and 'I can't tell' fits someone who has never tried it.
screens.why5: The product name appears only as part of the idea being shown on purpose, and nothing here adds a founder's plan or a label for me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four brief options I can hold after hearing them once, and the escape comes last in a few words.

screens.why1: After being told about the idea and asked if it would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I would actually wear the glasses with my phone.
screens.why2: Glasses paired to a phone is plain to me, since I already deal with pairing hearing aids or other gear to my phone, and I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know how I feel about wearing glasses in conversation and about keeping devices connected, because dropped Bluetooth is something I already live with.
screens.why4: The set covers my answers and the escape fits, but 'Probably not' and 'No' sit close together, and the pairing option is a long, specific condition that leaves out other reasons, such as how the glasses look or feel.
screens.why5: It is shown openly as the idea I was asked to imagine, and it describes wearing the glasses paired to a phone without any company talk about people like me.
screens.why6: The question says well and the list is short, but 'Only if pairing took a minute and stayed connected' is a mouthful beside the one-word options, and it is not parallel with them.
screens.instead: To use AirCaps, you'd wear the glasses, paired to your phone. Would you do that, or not? Yes; Yes, if pairing stays reliable; Probably not; or No. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: I had just said I'd wear the glasses only if pairing was quick and stayed connected, so it makes sense to ask me about that condition right here.
screens.why2: The words are simple, but "for that to be true" is a bit knotty and I'd read it twice to work out if it wants tech details or what I'd need to see.
screens.why3: I know what happens when my hearing aids or other Bluetooth gear drop out, but I've never used these glasses, so what would make them pair fast and stay on is partly a guess.
screens.why4: There are no options, just a box to type in.
screens.why5: It only plays back my own condition about pairing and staying connected, and nothing new about the product or the company reaches me.
screens.why6: It is two short sentences with no symbols or lists, one question at the end, and easy to take in if heard once, though I'd want the words on screen as well.
screens.instead: You said only if pairing took a minute and stayed connected. What would you need to see to believe that?
